## What is an AI marketing engineer?

An AI marketing engineer does two jobs that are usually split: they write the go-to-market strategy, and they build the AI systems that execute it. One person designs the positioning and ships the inbound, content, and outbound systems that run it. Flow AI's practitioner rule: claims ship with receipts — the systems are public on GitHub, and client results are only published with real names and real numbers.

## What does AI marketing cost in New Zealand?

Flow AI prices by department: a fixed-scope one-week install, then a monthly run that can be cancelled at any time. Current figures come with the first read.

## AI Marketing for Small Business in NZ: The Complete Guide (2026)

Source URL: https://www.flowai.co.nz/blog/ai-marketing-for-small-business-nz.html
Type: Guide
Author: Amber Lan (Flow AI)
Published: 2026-08-20
Last updated: 2026-08-20

Guides

# AI marketing for small business in NZ: the complete guide.

AI marketing means using AI systems to run the repetitive parts of marketing, so a business without a marketing hire can still show up consistently: found on Google, cited by AI assistants, publishing every week, and following up with every lead. This guide covers what that includes, what it costs, and where to start.

By Amber Lan, AI marketing engineer. Last updated 20 August 2026.

Share guide

## Why AI changes the marketing math for NZ small businesses

The old math was brutal. A small business could not justify a full-time marketer, so the owner did the marketing personally, in the gaps between actual work. Content went out when there was time, which meant rarely. SEO was something the website person mentioned once. Leads got followed up when someone remembered. The result was a business that was good at its job and invisible to everyone who had not already heard of it.

AI changes which parts of that need a human. Adoption reflects it: in the U.S. Chamber of Commerce's 2025 Empowering Small Business report, the share of small businesses using generative AI jumped from 40% to 58% in a single year. The pattern in New Zealand looks the same from where I sit: the owners I talk to already use ChatGPT for one-off tasks. The gap is between using AI occasionally and having it run a system.

Here is the distinction that matters, and the one most AI marketing content glosses over. AI removes repetitive work. It does not remove judgment. Drafting fifty product descriptions is repetitive work. Deciding what your business should claim, and to whom, is judgment. A system that automates the first and leaves you the second makes one person as productive as a small team. A system that pretends to automate both produces the generic sludge you already recognise in your inbox.

## The four things AI marketing actually covers

Strip away the vendor noise and AI marketing for a small business is four systems. Each one can stand alone. Together they cover the whole funnel.

### 1. SEO: being found on Google

Still the foundation. Most NZ buying journeys start with a search, and the basics have not changed: a technically healthy site, pages that answer what people actually type, and business information that is consistent everywhere it appears. What AI changes is the cost of the work. Auditing, fixing metadata, writing location and service pages, and maintaining structured data used to be billable hours; now they are largely system output that a human reviews.

Concretely, for a NZ service business that means: every service you offer gets its own page written the way customers search ("gutter cleaning north shore" rather than "our services"), your Google Business Profile stays complete and current, and the technical layer that most owners never see, from page titles to schema markup, is generated and checked by the system instead of waiting for a web developer's next free week.

### 2. AEO and GEO: being cited by ChatGPT and AI search

The new layer, and the one almost no NZ small business has touched. When someone asks ChatGPT, Perplexity, or Google's AI Overviews to recommend a business that does what you do, the assistant answers with names. Getting into that answer is called answer engine optimization, and it is engineering rather than magic: let the AI crawlers in, describe your business in structured data, publish content that can be quoted in isolation, and keep your facts consistent across the web. I run an open-source toolkit for exactly this, and this website is its live demonstration.

The reason to move on this now is simple: the space is nearly empty. Very few NZ businesses have made themselves legible to AI assistants, which means the ones that do are competing against absence. In every other marketing channel you fight incumbents with budgets. In this one, for the moment, you mostly fight nobody.

### 3. A content engine: publishing without a content team

Consistency beats brilliance in small-business content, and consistency is exactly what a solo operator cannot sustain by hand. A content engine fixes the math: one source document goes in, and a month of platform-shaped posts comes out, each checked against codified brand-voice rules before anything ships. The owner's job collapses from writing everything to approving what a system drafted. I have written up how the one I run in production works, including why the quality gate matters more than the generation.

What goes in as the source matters more than owners expect. A recorded voice memo about a job that went sideways, a customer question you answered by email, a before-and-after from last week: these are the raw material of content people actually read, because they contain things only you know. The engine's job is to shape them per platform; your job is to keep noticing them.

### 4. Outbound automation: follow-up that never forgets

Most small businesses do not lose deals to competitors. They lose them to silence: the quote that never got a follow-up, the enquiry that sat over a busy weekend. Outbound automation covers prospect research, personalised first contact inside safe sending limits, and follow-up sequences that stop the moment a human replies. The hard rule that keeps it trustworthy: automation opens doors, a person walks through them.

For a small B2B business this typically means a short, honest first email to a well-researched list, a polite follow-up or two, and instant handover to you the moment anyone answers. No fake personalisation, no pressure sequences. The win is coverage: every lead and lapsed customer hears from you, which is more than most competitors manage.

## What a week looks like when the systems run

Theory aside, here is roughly how a week runs once the four systems are live, based on how I operate the same stack in production.

Monday, about an hour. Review the content packet the engine drafted from last week's source material. Approve most of it, rewrite the two pieces where the judgment call matters, schedule the lot. Skim the weekend's enquiries and check the follow-up system caught them all.

Midweek, in the gaps. Answer the replies outbound generated, because a human always takes over the moment a buyer engages. Capture one piece of raw material for next week's content: a customer question, a job story, a number worth sharing.

Friday, half an hour. Read the one-page report: what shipped, what moved, which channel produced this week's conversations. Decide one adjustment for next week. That is the whole management overhead.

The point of the walkthrough is the shape of the owner's time. Almost none of it is production. Nearly all of it is judgment, which is the part only you can do, and the part that was always the actual value of marketing.

## How to choose your first system

If you only build one thing this quarter, pick it by where your next customer actually comes from.

- Local service business (trades, clinics, home services): start with SEO plus AI-search visibility. Your buyers search with intent and location; being the answer wins the job before anyone else quotes.

- B2B with a defined buyer (consultancies, software, wholesale): start with outbound. A small, well-researched list with reliable follow-up beats months of content while your pipeline is empty.

- Expertise business (advisors, agencies, specialists): start with the content engine. Your buying decision is a trust decision, and consistent published judgment is how strangers learn to trust you.

- Already getting traffic that does not convert: start with analytics and follow-up before spending anything on more visibility. Fix the leak before paying for more water.

## What this costs against an agency, a freelancer, or a hire

The honest answer is that every option can work, and each has a structural trade-off. Prices for agencies and freelancers vary widely in NZ, so get current quotes rather than trusting anyone's summary of the market, including mine. What I can compare is the structure of what you pay for.

Option

What you pay for

Structural trade-off

Agency

A team's hours across your account, usually on a monthly retainer with a minimum term.

Breadth of skills, but your budget buys hours, and small retainers get junior hours. The work usually stops when the invoice does.

Freelancer

One specialist's time, per project or per hour.

Strong in their lane, but marketing needs several lanes, and coordinating freelancers becomes your job.

In-house hire

A salary, plus tools, plus management time.

Full attention on your business, at the highest fixed cost, and one person still cannot cover strategy, content, SEO, and outbound by hand.

Fractional marketer

Senior judgment, a day or two a week.

Excellent strategy, but execution still needs hands or budget on top.

AI systems + one engineer

Systems that do the production, one accountable person doing the judgment. Flow AI's version is public: NZ$997 one-time for one system, or NZ$1,000/month for the full engine.

Depth of a team's output at one person's price. The trade-off is trust: the model only works if the operator shows receipts, which is why mine are public on GitHub.

## A practical starting checklist

You do not need all four systems on day one. This is the order that compounds.

### Week 1: find out where you stand

- Ask ChatGPT and Google to recommend a business that does what you do, in your town. Note who comes up. That is your real competition for the new front page.

- Run a basic health check on your own site: does it load fast, does every page have a clear title and description, does it say plainly what you do and where?

- If you want a structured version of this step, my free AI-readiness benchmark takes two minutes and needs no email.

### Weeks 2 to 4: fix the basics

- Make your business information identical everywhere: site, Google Business Profile, directories, social bios.

- Let the AI crawlers in via robots.txt and add structured data that says who you are, what you sell, and where you serve.

- Publish honest answers to the questions buyers actually ask, one page per real question.

### Month 2 and on: build the cadence

- Stand up a content rhythm you can sustain forever, even if that is one good piece a week. A system helps precisely here.

- Wire up follow-up: every enquiry gets a response path that does not depend on your memory.

- Measure. One page of numbers a month tells you which channel pays. Without it you are guessing.

## Common mistakes NZ small businesses make with AI marketing

Buying tools without a system. A ChatGPT subscription is not a marketing function. Tools produce output; a system decides what to produce, checks the quality, and ships it on schedule. The tool spend is wasted without the surrounding discipline.

Ignoring AI search entirely. Optimising only for Google in 2026 is optimising for part of the front page. The assistants answer with names either way; the only question is whether yours is one of them.

Publishing unreviewed AI output. Readers recognise generated text faster every month, and nothing burns trust quicker. Every line should pass a human or a codified quality gate before it carries your name.

Doing everything at once. Four systems launched simultaneously by one busy owner means four systems abandoned by June. Sequence them. The checklist above is the order I use with clients.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is AI marketing for a small business?

Using AI systems to run the repetitive parts of marketing: drafting content, keeping SEO and AI-search visibility healthy, researching and contacting prospects, and reporting. The owner keeps the judgment calls; the systems do the production. Done well, one person can run what used to need a team.

### How much does AI marketing cost for a small NZ business?

It ranges from a few software subscriptions if you run tools yourself, up to agency-level retainers if you outsource everything. Flow AI publishes its pricing as a reference point: a NZ$997 one-time starter sprint, or NZ$1,000 per month for the full engine, cancel anytime, with a 30-day money-back guarantee on the first month.

### Do I still need SEO if I am doing AEO?

Yes. Answer engine optimization builds on SEO rather than replacing it. AI assistants read the same web Google crawls, and several draw on search indexes directly. A technically healthy, clearly structured site is the starting condition for both; AEO adds the layer that makes your content quotable and machine-readable.

### Can one person really run all of this?

Yes, if the systems come first. One person cannot hand-write a month of content and research fifty prospects a week. One person can review what systems produce and make the judgment calls. That is the design principle this whole guide rests on: machines do production, the human does strategy and quality control.

## Three demand engines, one pipeline, one launch · Case study · Flow AI

Source URL: https://www.flowai.co.nz/work/enterprise-gtm.html
Type: Case study
Author: Amber Lan (Flow AI)
Published: 2026-08-20
Last updated: 2026-08-20

Case study

# Three demand engines, one pipeline, one launch.

A complete go-to-market system for an enterprise AI platform: outbound, inbound and partnership engines feeding one measured pipeline, aimed at a single launch moment.

Designed and operated by one person, in production at the AI startup where I run marketing. By Amber Lan, AI marketing engineer. Last updated 20 August 2026.

Back to selected work

## The problem.

An enterprise AI platform two quarters from a hard launch window, with no marketing team.

### No position, no engines

Positioning undecided, no message architecture, nothing running. Enterprise buyers research through analysts, peers, search and AI assistants, so a single channel was never going to hold.

### One operator, no agency

Every system had to run solo: automated where machines are better, human only where judgment matters. An enterprise audience punishes overpromising, so every public claim needed a source or it did not ship.

## What was built.

Three engines converge on one CRM pipeline, so every channel is measured against the same definition of a qualified conversation.

### Outbound

Signal-triggered research and personalised outreach inside safe sending limits. Automation stops the moment a buyer replies.

### Inbound

Search and answer-engine visibility, plus a content engine producing platform-native artefacts from single source documents.

### Partnerships

A lighthouse program that gives early customers a co-marketing reason to go public.

Underneath: a claims register holding every public claim with its evidence and status, a message architecture mapping claims to buyer roles, and an operating timeline sequencing all of it toward one launch moment.

## Key decisions.

Four calls that made the system operable by one person.

### One launch moment, not a drip

Enterprise attention compounds when the category claim, the proof and the availability land together.

### The claims register before the copy

Writing became fast because what could be said was already settled.

### Engines that keep running

Systems over campaigns. Nothing in the plan stops working when a sprint ends.

### Human takeover as a hard rule

The moment a person replies, automation stands down. Trust is easier to keep than to win back.

## The result.

The plan lives as a navigable deck the leadership team uses, and the engines it specifies are in production.

### In production

Positioning, message architecture, channel design and the operating timeline, run by the person who designed them, feeding one pipeline ahead of launch. Real numbers publish here once the launch window closes, not before.

### Evidence

A sanitised case: the company's identity and internal numbers stay private, and the full walkthrough is available on a call. Public: the clean-room content engine behind the inbound side, and the role where the system runs today.

### What I learned

Sequencing beats volume. The same assets, landed in order against one launch moment, do more than twice the assets scattered across a quarter. A claims register is the highest-leverage marketing document nobody writes.

Tell me what you do and where the pipeline stalls. You get a written read within the first week.

## A content engine with a codified voice gate · Case study · Flow AI

Source URL: https://www.flowai.co.nz/work/content-engine.html
Type: Case study
Author: Amber Lan (Flow AI)
Published: 2026-08-20
Last updated: 2026-08-20

Case study

# One source in. A month of publishable content out.

A content engine that turns one source document into platform-native posts, where every line passes a codified voice audit before it ships.

Built in Python on Claude agents. Clean-room version public on GitHub. By Amber Lan, AI marketing engineer. Last updated 20 August 2026.

Back to selected work

One source fans out to LinkedIn, X, blog, email and cards. Nothing passes the gate until it survives the voice audit.

## The problem.

One person cannot hand-write platform-native content at volume, and raw model output reads generated.

### Quality control at scale

The tells are recognisable, the voice drifts, and the volume meant to build trust starts eroding it. The problem is not generation.

### Voice as law, not vibes

Rules a machine can check, written down. Zero tolerance for recognisable AI patterns. Each platform gets its native shape, not one post cross-pasted five ways. The pipeline runs solo inside a bigger operating week.

## What was built.

Source document in, a packet of platform-shaped posts out, ready for a human yes or no.

### Plan

The engine plans a skeleton per artefact and generates platform-native drafts.

### Audit

Every line runs through a voice gate: banned words and patterns, sentence rhythm, claim discipline, and the brand's specific rules.

### Rewrite

Artefacts that fail are rewritten against the specific violations, not regenerated blind.

## Key decisions.

Four calls that moved the engineering to where it matters.

### The audit is the product

Generation is cheap. The gate makes the output shippable, so most of the engineering lives there.

### Voice as law, not prompt

Style guidance in a prompt decays. Codified rules checked line by line do not.

### Human approves, machine produces

The operator's job collapsed from writing to judging, the only part that needed a human.

### Packets, not posts

One source becomes a coordinated set across platforms, so the calendar fills in one pass.

## The result.

In production, one source document reliably becomes a month of on-brand, platform-native content.

### In production

The operator's time goes to judgment instead of drafting. Packaged as a reusable skill: a new brand means codifying its voice rules, not rebuilding the pipeline.

### Evidence

The clean-room version is public: read the code on GitHub. The distribution half is public too: Social Media OS.

### What I learned

Generated content fails at the last metre, in the lines a reader flags as machine-made. Fixing that at the gate, line by line, separates a content engine from a content faucet.

## Want a system like this pointed at your business?

Tell me what you do and where the pipeline stalls. You get a written read within the first week.

## A toolkit that optimises for AI citations, not just rankings · Case study · Flow AI

Source URL: https://www.flowai.co.nz/work/geo-seo-toolkit.html
Type: Case study
Author: Amber Lan (Flow AI)
Published: 2026-08-20
Last updated: 2026-08-20

Case study

# Built so the machines cite you, not just rank you.

geo-seo-claude is a GEO/AEO-first SEO toolkit: citability scoring, AI-crawler access analysis, schema markup generation and reports.

Being cited by ChatGPT, Claude and Perplexity is the target; Google rankings are one input. Public on GitHub and running on this site. By Amber Lan, AI marketing engineer. Last updated 20 August 2026.

Back to selected work

A site is scored for citability, then tuned until ChatGPT, Claude and Perplexity can find, parse and quote it.

## The problem.

Buyers ask AI assistants for recommendations, and assistants answer with names.

### The gap in classic SEO

Rankings and backlinks say nothing about whether an AI crawler can reach a site, whether the content is quotable in isolation, or whether the structured data says who the business is. Small businesses lose the new front page in that gap.

### Checks, not vibes

Crawler access is testable, schema parses or it does not, and a citability score needs stated criteria. It had to run as a practitioner tool inside Claude Code, on a real client site, in minutes.

## What was built.

The toolkit audits a site the way an answer engine consumes it, then generates the fixes it recommends.

### Crawler access

The nine AI agents that matter, from GPTBot to PerplexityBot, plus llms.txt presence and quality.

### Structure

Structured-data coverage and answer-first content structure.

### Citability

Passage-level citability scoring, then the fixes: robots rules, JSON-LD schema and a report a client can act on.

## Key decisions.

Three calls that change what gets fixed first.

### Citability as the metric

A page that ranks but cannot be quoted in isolation loses the AI answer. Scoring quotability changes what you fix first.

### Crawler access before content

If GPTBot or PerplexityBot is blocked, nothing else matters, so the audit starts there.

### Generate fixes, not findings

A report that ships the corrected robots.txt and schema blocks gets implemented. A list of problems gets filed.

## The result.

The proof is recursive: this website runs the toolkit's own playbook.

### Live proof

flowai.co.nz allows all nine AI crawlers, serves llms.txt at the root and under .well-known, carries JSON-LD on every page, and structures answers for extraction. The Flow AI retainer applies the same toolkit to client sites.

### Evidence

Read the toolkit on GitHub. Inspect the live implementation: robots.txt, llms.txt, and the structured data in this page's source.

### What I learned

Answer-engine optimisation is discipline, not tricks: let the crawlers in, say who you are in schema, lead with the answer, keep claims sourced. The toolkit makes that discipline repeatable.

Tell me what you do and where the pipeline stalls. You get a written read within the first week.

## Questions.

### What is an AI marketing engineer?

An AI marketing engineer connects go-to-market strategy to the systems that execute it. The role combines positioning, search visibility, content operations, outbound automation, and measurement.

### How is Flow AI different from a marketing agency?

You work directly with the practitioner who writes the strategy and builds the systems. There are no account-manager handoffs, and the work is designed to keep operating after launch.

### How quickly can the first system go live?

The written go-to-market read arrives within the first week, and the first agreed system is designed to go live in week one.

### Who is Flow AI for?

Early-stage teams and small businesses in Australia and New Zealand that need senior marketing thinking and hands-on execution without hiring a full internal function.

### What does AI marketing cost in Australia and New Zealand?

Flow AI prices by department: a fixed-scope one-week install, then a monthly run that can be cancelled at any time. Current figures come with the first read, so you see the number against your own situation rather than a rate card.

### What is AI-search optimisation?

AI-search optimisation, also called answer engine optimisation (AEO) or generative engine optimisation (GEO), is the practice of structuring a website so AI assistants such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity cite it when answering buyers' questions. Research presented at KDD 2024 by Aggarwal et al. found that adding quotations to a page improved its visibility in AI-generated answers by up to 41 percent, and adding statistics by up to 33 percent.
